title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Lecture and Q&A with students of Peking University (Guanghua School of Mgmt.)
summary: Speaking in shorts to visiting Peking University students in Irvine, Pabrai contrasts 'great businesses' with 'great investments' through two 12-year contests: Sunteck Realty vs Guy Spier's MasterCard, and Rain Industries vs Motherson Sumi. He argues the real edge lies in finding hidden moats that analysts do not yet see, explains his no-team, open-source idea flow, and discusses the differences between investing in India and the US.

ideas.idea: Take the job you would do if you were not getting paid; choosing a career for pay or prestige is the wrong decision.
ideas.detail: His trainer Jason said that after winning a $500 million Powerball he would still come to the club; Pabrai runs an $800 million fund in shorts and Nike sneakers because he would do it unpaid.

ideas.idea: Run an empty calendar like Buffett and Munger and be very good at saying no.
ideas.detail: Peking U was the only item on his calendar that week; he has about 400 investors and cannot remember his last call or email with any of them, copying Buffett's partnership practice of being available one day a year with semi-annual letters.

ideas.idea: Cloning is one of the most important models: when you see someone doing something smart, just incorporate it.
ideas.detail: He could not have come up with the empty calendar or investor-communication ideas himself; he copied them from Warren and Charlie.

ideas.idea: It is not about the great business, it is about the great investment; a mediocre company can be a great investment and vice versa.
ideas.detail: If investing were just about identifying the best-quality businesses it would be a simple game because everyone can see which businesses are great and prices them accordingly.

ideas.idea: A 12-year contest started October 14, 2018 pits Guy Spier's MasterCard ($204/share, $212B cap, 42x trailing PE) against Sunteck Realty (under $700M cap).
ideas.detail: Guy's $1 million in MasterCard became $12 million but will not become $144 million in the next 12 years. Through May 2019 MasterCard was up 25% and Sunteck up 38%. He runs about 10 such contests to shake up people who conflate great companies with great investments.

ideas.idea: Sunteck Realty was bought at about 100 rupees after India's 2016 demonetization when its market cap of under $200M was below the $500M value of a single project of 60 finished Mumbai apartments.
ideas.detail: Demonetization, RERA and GST wiped out 90% of Indian developers, leaving clean operators like Sunteck among only 8-10 players who will rebuild Mumbai over 30-40 years. He bought 9.999% (the maximum allowed) and the stock rose almost 5x to 460-500 in three years.

ideas.idea: The starting price you pay matters: Coca-Cola at 40x earnings in 2000 returned under 3% a year through 2018 even though it stayed a great business.
ideas.detail: Berkshire's Coke went up 12-14x from 1988 to 2000, then the multiple compressed from over 40 to 17. Buffett later acknowledged not selling around 2001-2002 was probably a mistake, though he prefers to be a collector of great businesses and Berkshire's cash math differs.

ideas.idea: Moutai has the ultimate moat and is very hard to disrupt, whereas MasterCard's 2% take rate could be disrupted the way Chinese payment systems already bypass it.
ideas.detail: Moutai has a thousand-year history, is embedded in people's heads, holds large inventory and keeps raising prices with China's rise; he owns Moutai but notes it is fully priced because everyone knows the story.

ideas.idea: Motherson Sumi has an incredible, unusual moat: automakers like BMW call it to rescue failing suppliers and pay it to take them over.
ideas.detail: Chaand Sehgal never solicits acquisitions; BMW writes a ~$100M cheque plus a supply contract, he replaces the plant head with an under-35 insider, never relocates plants, and the plant is profitable within a year. Stock went from 9 cents at 1994 IPO to 146, about 30% annualized; of about 200 Indian CEOs he met, none is better, yet he does not own it at 27x trailing PE.

ideas.idea: Rain Industries was bought at 35 rupees in 2015 for a $200M market cap when he judged it would earn $200M a year within three or four years; it hit 450 rupees in 2018.
ideas.detail: A stranger in Vancouver emailed a 20-page PDF; three hours later he told his broker to buy every share and reached 9.999%. Rain supplies coal tar pitch and calcined coke to aluminum smelters in a two-or-three-player oligopoly with long-term contracts. Even after the fall it is a 3x, at 6x earnings.

ideas.idea: Rain's CEO did brilliant public LBOs, borrowing $1.5 billion of non-recourse high-yield debt to buy businesses 5-10x his size with nothing down.
ideas.detail: In 2008 Rain bought a $1B US business at 11-12% interest, later a $700M European business with the debt placed on the first one, then refinanced to 5.5%. Recent capex of $140M generates $100M pretax a year, and reinvesting at such rates could make Rain a $400-500M-a-year earner.

ideas.idea: The most exciting investments are hidden moats: great businesses no one else sees yet, bought before the 30 analysts arrive.
ideas.detail: MasterCard, Motherson Sumi and Moutai are followed by 30 analysts so there is no mispricing; Rain is unfollowed and may be viewed like Motherson in 5-10 years, at which point it could trade at 30x earnings.

ideas.idea: You only truly learn a business after you own it, not when you analyze it.
ideas.detail: He bought Rain in 2015 planning to make 5x and sell, but after owning it for three years and meeting the reclusive CEO in Hyderabad, he now wants to hold Rain and Sunteck for 10-15 years as an owner.

ideas.idea: His earlier framework of buying at a 50-60% discount and selling in three years has the flaw that you must keep finding new ideas and pay a lot of tax; buying great businesses with long runways cheaply is better.
ideas.detail: He admits that in 25 years he has not paid as much attention to great businesses as he should have, though unlike Guy Spier he will never go into preservation mode and wants to 'hit it out of the park'.

ideas.idea: In small owner-run companies like Sunteck and Rain the key-person risk is real: if something happens to the operator, he would have to exit.
ideas.detail: For MasterCard it does not matter who runs it; for Rain and Sunteck the bet is that the operator is phenomenal, so he must watch that risk.

ideas.idea: Even the best investor makes mistakes, and in investing you can be wrong 40% of the time and still do very well.
ideas.detail: Cited in the context of Buffett not selling Coke in 2001.

ideas.idea: He needs no analysts because he only needs two or three stocks a year; his source is open source, with ideas emailed by strangers.
ideas.detail: Buffett and Munger have zero analysts. Of 50,000 stocks, at least 3,000 are severely underpriced and he needs to understand only three or four. Rain came from a stranger in Vancouver whom he later took to dim sum; he also watches what Li Lu does.

ideas.idea: Be unreasonable and a harsh grader: if everything is not perfect, say no and toss it.
ideas.detail: One of his 10 commandments; with governance issues you should just pass because you are fighting an uphill battle. He is not only a small-cap investor, having recently bought Micron (over $40B cap) and Fiat Chrysler (over $20B).

ideas.idea: Assess whether a wealthy promoter still has the drive to grow: he asked Sunteck's 68% owner whether he aspires to turn $1 billion into $10 billion.
ideas.detail: Rain's family owns 40% and has zero interest in money; they just want to keep going. Many small companies never become big because capitalism is brutal.

ideas.idea: In India he never invests without kicking the tires because of fraud risk, whereas in the US he never meets management.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: He has sat in meetings with Indian companies that were obvious frauds; India's promoters often ignore outside shareholders, so clean accounting, honest auditors and governance must be verified. The same adjustment likely applies to China.

ideas.idea: India offers more gaps between price and value because companies are under-followed, while the US shrank from 8,000 to 3,600 public companies with far more analysts.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: It is much harder to find value gaps in the US than in India, so the tool set must be adjusted per market.

ideas.idea: Investors should value businesses on the actual operating record, not the stock chart.
ideas.detail: Rain's chart was flat from 1991 to 2015, but the record showed bold acquisitions, bankers willing to lend $1B to an Indian company, cyclical trough earnings that were still positive, and consistently well-executed capital projects.
